claim: The study characterized 1,280 infections from the National Basketball Association occupational health cohort identified between June 2020 and January 2022 using serial RT-qPCR testing.
source: We characterized 1,280 infections from the National Basketball Association occupational health cohort identified between June 2020 and January 2022 using serial RT-qPCR testing.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and describes the study dataset.

claim: Among individuals detected partway through their infection, 51.0% (95% credible interval [CrI]: 48.3–53.6%) remained potentially infectious (Ct <30) 5 days post detection.
source: Among individuals detected partway through their infection, 51.0% (95% credible interval [CrI]: 48.3–53.6%) remained potentially infectious (Ct <30) 5 days post detection, with small differences across variants and vaccination status.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's analysis of Ct values over time.

claim: Only seven viral rebounds (0.7%; N=999) were observed with rebound defined as 3+days with Ct <30 following an initial clearance of 3+days with Ct ≥30.
source: Only seven viral rebounds (0.7%; N=999) were observed, with rebound defined as 3+days with Ct <30 following an initial clearance of 3+days with Ct ≥30.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the study data using a specific definition of viral rebound.

claim: High antibody titers against the founder SARS-CoV-2 strain predicted lower peak viral loads and shorter durations of infection.
source: High antibody titers against the founder SARS-CoV-2 strain predicted lower peak viral loads and shorter durations of infection.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis of antibody titers and viral kinetics.

claim: Among Omicron BA.1 infections, boosted individuals had lower pre-booster antibody titers and longer clearance times than non-boosted individuals.
source: Among Omicron BA.1 infections, boosted individuals had lower pre-booster antibody titers and longer clearance times than non-boosted individuals.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis comparing boosted and non-boosted individuals.

claim: The amount and duration of viral shedding influences infectiousness.
source: The amount and duration of viral shedding influences infectiousness (Ke et al., 2021; Ke et al., 2022; Marc et al., 2021; Marks et al., 2021; Puhach et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The duration of test positivity affects isolation policies, test recommendations, and clinical care guidelines.
source: the duration of test positivity affect isolation policies, test recommendations, and clinical care guidelines (Hellewell et al., 2021; Kissler et al., 2021a; Larremore et al., 2021; Mack et al., 2022; Néant et al., 2021; Quilty et al., 2021; Singanayagam et al., 2022)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Rebounds of viral RNA concentrations and symptoms have been observed after antiviral treatment.
source: rebounds of viral RNA concentrations and symptoms have been observed after antiviral treatment, but it has been unclear to what extent such rebounds also occur in the absence of drug (Boucau et al., 2022b; Charness et al., 2022)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on rebounds after antiviral treatment.

claim: Most longitudinal viral kinetics studies pre-date the emergence of the Omicron variant.
source: Most longitudinal viral kinetics studies pre-date the emergence of the Omicron variant, which features dramatic antigenic divergence from prior variants, as well as the rollout of third and fourth vaccine doses (Lusvarghi et al., 2022; van der Straten et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and describes the state of prior research.

claim: The Omicron variant features dramatic antigenic divergence from prior variants.
source: Most longitudinal viral kinetics studies pre-date the emergence of the Omicron variant, which features dramatic antigenic divergence from prior variants, as well as the rollout of third and fourth vaccine doses (Lusvarghi et al., 2022; van der Straten et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on Omicron's antigenic properties.

claim: Clinical samples were obtained by combined swabs of the anterior nares and oropharynx.
source: Clinical samples were obtained by combined swabs of the anterior nares and oropharynx, collected separately from each anatomical site, for each patient administered by a trained provider.
evidence: This describes the sample collection methodology used in the study.

claim: Cycle threshold (Ct) values were generated using the Roche cobas target 1 assay.
source: Cycle threshold (Ct) values were generated using the Roche cobas target 1 assay.
evidence: This describes the assay used for generating Ct values in the study.

claim: The threshold of Ct <30 was chosen based on a combination of antigen sensitivity and studies of virus culture by Ct.
source: This threshold was chosen based on a combination of antigen sensitivity and studies of virus culture by Ct, where the presence of culturable virus is often assumed to correlate with infectivity (Brihn et al., 2021; Bullard et al., 2020; Pilarowski et al., 2021; Singanayagam et al., 2020; Thommes et al., 2021).
evidence: This explains the rationale for the Ct threshold choice, supported by citations.

claim: The presence of culturable virus is often assumed to correlate with infectivity.
source: This threshold was chosen based on a combination of antigen sensitivity and studies of virus culture by Ct, where the presence of culturable virus is often assumed to correlate with infectivity (Brihn et al., 2021; Bullard et al., 2020; Pilarowski et al., 2021; Singanayagam et al., 2020; Thommes et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a general assumption in the field, supported by citations.

claim: 828 individuals had been boosted by the time of their last PCR test.
source: 828 individuals had been boosted by the time of their last PCR test, 529 had completed their primary vaccination course (two doses of an mRNA vaccine or one dose of Janssen / Ad.26.COV2.S adenovirus vector-based vaccine), 8 had received one vaccine dose, and 13 confirmed to be unvaccinated.
evidence: This is a direct count from the study cohort.

claim: 529 individuals had completed their primary vaccination course.
source: 828 individuals had been boosted by the time of their last PCR test, 529 had completed their primary vaccination course (two doses of an mRNA vaccine or one dose of Janssen / Ad.26.COV2.S adenovirus vector-based vaccine), 8 had received one vaccine dose, and 13 confirmed to be unvaccinated.
evidence: This is a direct count from the study cohort.

claim: All sequenced Omicron infections were lineage BA.1 apart from 1 BA.2.10 infection.
source: All sequenced Omicron infections were lineage BA.1 apart from 1 BA.2.10 infection.
evidence: This is a finding from the genome sequencing analysis.

claim: Sequenced Delta infections were a combination of lineages B.1.617.2 and AY.x.
source: Sequenced Delta infections were a combination of lineages B.1.617.2 and AY.x.
evidence: This is a finding from the genome sequencing analysis.

claim: Individuals were tested with the Diasorin Trimeric Assay for IgG antibody titers against the ancestral SARS-CoV-2 (WA1) strain spike protein during the 2021 pre-season period (September-October 2021).
source: Individuals were tested with the Diasorin Trimeric Assay for IgG antibody titers against the ancestral SARS-CoV-2 (WA1) strain spike protein during the 2021 pre-season period (September-October 2021).
evidence: This describes the antibody testing methodology and timing.

claim: An authentic virus neutralization titer of 100 was found to be well correlated with a 50% protective neutralization level for wildtype.
source: Specifically, an authentic virus neutralization titer of 100 was found to be well correlated with a 50% protective neutralization level for wildtype (Khoury et al., 2021) and found to correspond to a DiaSorin AU of 189.09 (95%CI: 147.61–235.75) (Appendix 1—figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and reference to a figure in the manuscript.

claim: The cutoff of 250 AU/ml was chosen as a conservative upper bound classifying an individual as at lower risk of infection with Delta or wildtype SARS-CoV-2.
source: The cutoff of 250 was therefore chosen as a conservative upper bound classifying an individual as at lower risk of infection with Delta or wildtype SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This explains the rationale for the antibody titer cutoff choice.

claim: The cutoff of 250 AU/ml does not predict infection risk with Omicron.
source: Note that this cutoff does not predict infection risk with Omicron and was simply chosen as a proxy for an individual's immune competence.
evidence: This is an explicit limitation stated by the authors.

claim: Most individuals (posterior mean: 65.4%, 95% credible intervals [CrI]: 62.0–68.8%) in the frequent testing group remained potentially infectious on day 5 post detection.
source: Most individuals (posterior mean: 65.4%, 95% credible intervals [CrI]: 62.0–68.8%) in the frequent testing group remained potentially infectious on day 5 post detection.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the logistic regression model.

claim: In the frequent testing group, 20.0% (95% CrI: 17.3–22.8%) remained potentially infectious at day 10.
source: This fraction decreased to 20.0% (95% CrI: 17.3–22.8%) at day 10.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the logistic regression model.

claim: In the delayed detection group, the proportion with Ct <30 was 51.0% (95% credible interval (CrI): 48.3–53.6%) on day 5 post detection.
source: In this group, the proportion with Ct <30 was 51.0% (95% credible interval (CrI): 48.3–53.6%) on day 5 post detection and 9.37% (95% CrI: 7.98–10.9%) on day 10.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the logistic regression model.

claim: In the delayed detection group, 9.37% (95% CrI: 7.98–10.9%) remained potentially infectious on day 10.
source: In this group, the proportion with Ct <30 was 51.0% (95% credible interval (CrI): 48.3–53.6%) on day 5 post detection and 9.37% (95% CrI: 7.98–10.9%) on day 10.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the logistic regression model.

claim: 40 (3.00%) of 1,334 infections were identified as rebounds when only 2+consecutive days of Ct ≥30 followed by 2+days of Ct <30 was required.
source: For example, 40 (3.00%) of 1,334 infections were identified as rebounds when only 2+consecutive days of Ct ≥30 followed by 2+days of Ct <30 was required to be classified as such (Table 2; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the rebound analysis using a less stringent definition.

claim: Rebound infections were more likely in Omicron BA.1 infections, with 36 (4.10%; N=877) Omicron BA.1 infections resulting in rebound compared to one (0.562%; N=178) and three (1.08%; N=279) Delta and other infections, respectively.
source: Under this definition, we found that rebound infections were more likely in Omicron BA.1 infections, with 36 (4.10%; N=877) Omicron BA.1 infections resulting in rebound compared to one (0.562%; N=178) and three (1.08%; N=279) Delta and other infections, respectively (Appendix 1—table 1; Chi-squared test for Omicron BA.1 (N=877) vs. non-Omicron BA.1 infection (N=457), test statistic = 9.69, P-value <0.05).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the rebound analysis with statistical testing.

claim: Rebounds were more common in boosted individuals, with 32 (6.48%; N=494) rebounds in boosted individuals vs. three (0.929%; N=323) and two (1.26%; N=159) rebounds in vaccinated and unvaccinated individuals, respectively.
source: Similarly, we found that rebounds were more common in boosted individuals, with 32 (6.48%; N=494) rebounds in boosted individuals vs. three (0.929%; N=323) and two (1.26%; N=159) rebounds in vaccinated and unvaccinated individuals, respectively (Appendix 1—table 2; Chi-squared test for boosted (N=494) vs. not-boosted (N=478) infection, test statistic = 18.1, P-value <1e-4).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the rebound analysis with statistical testing.

claim: The baseline logistic regression model gave an overall classification accuracy for an individual having Ct <30 or ≥30/negative of 81.7% with an AUC of 88.6% for the frequent testing group.
source: The baseline model, which included only the number of days since detection as a predictor, gave an overall classification accuracy for an individual having Ct <30 or ≥30/negative of 81.7% with an AUC of 88.6% (group-level classification accuracies: Ct <30 = 60.6%; Ct ≥30/negative = 89.0%) for the frequent testing group, and an overall classification accuracy of 84.2% with an AUC of 90.5% (Ct <30 = 72.2%; Ct ≥30/negative = 88.0%) in the delayed detection group.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the model comparison analysis.

claim: The baseline logistic regression model gave an overall classification accuracy of 84.2% with an AUC of 90.5% in the delayed detection group.
source: The baseline model, which included only the number of days since detection as a predictor, gave an overall classification accuracy for an individual having Ct <30 or ≥30/negative of 81.7% with an AUC of 88.6% (group-level classification accuracies: Ct <30 = 60.6%; Ct ≥30/negative = 89.0%) for the frequent testing group, and an overall classification accuracy of 84.2% with an AUC of 90.5% (Ct <30 = 72.2%; Ct ≥30/negative = 88.0%) in the delayed detection group.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the model comparison analysis.

claim: The best model gave an overall classification accuracy of 82.8% with an AUC of 89.7% for the frequent testing group.
source: In contrast, the best model, which included the cumulative number of exposures, variant and age, gave an overall classification accuracy of 82.8% with an AUC of 89.7% (Ct <30 = 64.7%; Ct ≥30/negative = 89.0%) for the frequent testing group and an overall classification accuracy of 85.0% with an AUC of 91.4% (Ct <30 = 71.2%; Ct ≥30/negative = 89.3%) in the delayed detection group.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the model comparison analysis.

claim: The best model gave an overall classification accuracy of 85.0% with an AUC of 91.4% in the delayed detection group.
source: In contrast, the best model, which included the cumulative number of exposures, variant and age, gave an overall classification accuracy of 82.8% with an AUC of 89.7% (Ct <30 = 64.7%; Ct ≥30/negative = 89.0%) for the frequent testing group and an overall classification accuracy of 85.0% with an AUC of 91.4% (Ct <30 = 71.2%; Ct ≥30/negative = 89.3%) in the delayed detection group.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the model comparison analysis.

claim: Exposure histories provide little assistance in predicting an individual's course of infectiousness over time, due to a high degree of individual-level variation.
source: These results indicate that while exposure histories help to explain mean viral RNA kinetics, they provide little assistance in predicting an individual's course of infectiousness over time, due to a high degree of individual-level variation, which may be dominated by stochastic effects or other unmeasured characteristics.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model comparison results.

claim: Vaccination provides multiple layers of protection against SARS-CoV-2, leading to reduced rates of infection and faster clearance of the virus.
source: Vaccination provides multiple layers of protection against SARS-CoV-2, leading to reduced rates of infection (Tai et al., 2022) and faster clearance of the virus (Kissler et al., 2021b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Individuals who received two vaccine doses prior to infection with pre-Delta and pre-Omicron variants (N=12) cleared to negative results or high Ct values faster than unvaccinated individuals (N=209).
source: Consistent with these findings, individuals who received two vaccine doses prior to infection with pre-Delta and pre-Omicron variants (N=12) cleared to negative results or high Ct values faster than unvaccinated individuals (N=209) (Appendix 1—figure 9).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: Boosted individuals with Omicron BA.1 infections (N=615) tended to sustain low Ct values for longer durations than individuals who had only undergone an initial vaccine course (N=251).
source: While boosting reduced rates of infection in our cohort,(Tai et al., 2022) boosted individuals with Omicron BA.1 infections (N=615) tended to sustain low Ct values for longer durations than individuals who had only undergone an initial vaccine course (N=251), defined as either two doses of an mRNA vaccine or a single dose of the Ad.26.COV2.S adenovirus vector-based vaccine (Figure 2A; Appendix 1—figure 9).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis, with reference to figures.

claim: Boosting reduced rates of infection in the cohort.
source: While boosting reduced rates of infection in our cohort,(Tai et al., 2022) boosted individuals with Omicron BA.1 infections (N=615) tended to sustain low Ct values for longer durations than individuals who had only undergone an initial vaccine course (N=251), defined as either two doses of an mRNA vaccine or a single dose of the Ad.26.COV2.S adenovirus vector-based vaccine (Figure 2A; Appendix 1—figure 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on the same cohort.

claim: Boosted individuals in this cohort were typically older than non-boosted individuals at the time of BA.1 infection (mean age of 37.6 years in the BA-1 infected, boosted group vs. 31.3 years in the BA.1-infected, non-boosted group).
source: It is important to consider the possible confounding effect of age, as boosted individuals in this cohort were typically older than non-boosted individuals at the time of BA.1 infection (mean age of 37.6 years in the BA-1 infected, boosted group vs. 31.3 years in the BA.1-infected, non-boosted group).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the study cohort.

claim: Older individuals maintain Ct <30 for longer on average than younger individuals after conditioning on vaccination status.
source: The regression model including age group, vaccination status and variant found that older individuals do maintain Ct <30 for longer on average than younger individuals after conditioning on vaccination status (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from the regression model analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: The effect of a higher proportion with Ct <30 in boosted individuals relative to non-boosted individuals remained within each age group.
source: However, the effect of a higher proportion with Ct <30 in boosted individuals relative to non-boosted individuals also remained within each age group, suggesting that both older age and booster status explain some variation in duration of Ct <30 (Appendix 1—figure 12).
evidence: This is a finding from the regression model analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: 979 individuals were tested at least once (1,017 measurements total) with the Diasorin Trimeric Assay for antibody titers against the spike protein from the ancestral SARS-CoV-2 (WA1) strain.
source: In addition to exposure history information, 979 individuals were tested at least once (1,017 measurements total) with the Diasorin Trimeric Assay for antibody titers against the spike protein from the ancestral SARS-CoV-2 (WA1) strain (Appendix 1—figure 13).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic about the antibody testing in the cohort.

claim: Most titers were obtained from mid-September to mid-October 2021.
source: Most titers were obtained from mid-September to mid-October 2021, and thus we consider these titers to represent an individual's post primary vaccination course response rather than post-boost/post-Omicron infection immunity (Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: This describes the timing of antibody measurements in the study.

claim: The median time between the most recent vaccine dose and the titer draw was 162 days (interquartile range: 129–180 days).
source: The median time between the most recent vaccine dose and the titer draw was 162 days (interquartile range: 129–180 days) (Appendix 1—figure 14).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic about the timing of antibody measurements.

claim: 494 measurements were classified as low antibody titers (≤250 arbitrary units [AU]/ml) and 523 as high titers (>250 AU/ml).
source: A total of 494 measurements were classified as low antibody titers (≤250 arbitrary units [AU]/ml) and 523 as high titers (>250 AU/ml).
evidence: This describes the distribution of antibody titers in the cohort.

claim: Boosted individuals with a low antibody titer had the highest and longest duration of Ct <30 over time since detection in both the frequent testing and delayed detection group.
source: Boosted individuals with a low antibody titer had the highest and longest duration of Ct <30 over time since detection in both the frequent testing and delayed detection group.
evidence: This is a finding from the logistic regression model stratified by antibody titer.

claim: In the delayed detection group, individuals with low antibody titers were more likely to have Ct <30 than individuals with high antibody titers regardless of booster status.
source: In the delayed detection group, individuals with low antibody titers were more likely to have Ct <30 than individuals with high antibody titers regardless of booster status, though boosted individuals with high antibody titers maintained Ct <30 for longer than non-boosted individuals with low titers.
evidence: This is a finding from the logistic regression model stratified by antibody titer.

claim: Younger BA.1-infected individuals had higher antibody titers on average than older BA.1-infected individuals.
source: We found that younger BA.1-infected individuals had higher antibody titers on average than older BA.1-infected individuals, but that BA.1-infected boosted individuals had consistently lower mean antibody titers than BA.1-infected non-boosted individuals within each age group (Appendix 1—figure 15).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of antibody titers stratified by age and vaccination status.

claim: BA.1-infected boosted individuals had consistently lower mean antibody titers than BA.1-infected non-boosted individuals within each age group.
source: We found that younger BA.1-infected individuals had higher antibody titers on average than older BA.1-infected individuals, but that BA.1-infected boosted individuals had consistently lower mean antibody titers than BA.1-infected non-boosted individuals within each age group (Appendix 1—figure 15).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of antibody titers stratified by age and vaccination status.

claim: The trend of a higher and longer duration of Ct <30 in Omicron BA.1-infected, boosted, low titer individuals was maintained in sensitivity analyses restricting to specific time windows.
source: The trend of a higher and longer duration of Ct <30 in Omicron BA.1-infected, boosted, low titer individuals was maintained in both sensitivity analyses (Appendix 1—figure 16).
evidence: This describes the robustness of the finding to sensitivity analyses.

claim: Antibody titers were lower among fully vaccinated individuals who were subsequently infected with Delta than individuals who had been infected with a pre-Delta variant.
source: Antibody titers were lower among fully vaccinated individuals who were subsequently infected with Delta than individuals who had been infected with a pre-Delta variant.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of antibody titers stratified by variant and vaccination status.

claim: Mean antibody titers among Omicron BA.1-infected, fully vaccinated individuals were similar to individuals in the pre-Delta, unvaccinated group.
source: In contrast, we found that mean antibody titers among Omicron BA.1-infected, fully vaccinated individuals were similar to individuals in the pre-Delta, unvaccinated group, suggesting that higher titer individuals were not substantially less likely to be infected than lower titer individuals.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of antibody titers stratified by variant and vaccination status.

claim: Antibody titers were lowest among Omicron BA.1 infected boosted individuals.
source: Finally, we found that antibody titers were lowest among Omicron BA.1 infected boosted individuals, suggesting that individuals with a high titer measurement prior to being boosted were less likely to have Omicron BA.1 infections.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of antibody titers stratified by variant and vaccination status.

claim: Among Omicron BA.1 infections, boosted individuals had a longer estimated viral clearance time than non-boosted individuals (8.4 days (95% CrI: 8.0–8.7) vs. 6.2 days (95% CrI: 5.8–6.6), respectively).
source: According to the viral kinetic model, and among Omicron BA.1 infections, boosted individuals had a longer estimated viral clearance time than non-boosted individuals (8.4 days (95% CrI: 8.0–8.7) vs. 6.2 days (95% CrI: 5.8–6.6), respectively), in line with the results from the logistic regression model.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the viral kinetic model.

claim: Viral proliferation times and peak viral RNA were similar among boosted and non-boosted individuals with Omicron BA.1 infections.
source: Viral proliferation times and peak viral RNA were similar among boosted and non-boosted individuals with Omicron BA.1 infections (Appendix 1—table 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the viral kinetic model.

claim: Delta infections featured a consistently higher peak viral RNA than Omicron BA.1 infections when stratifying by post-initial vaccination antibody titer.
source: When stratifying by post-initial vaccination antibody titer, Delta infections featured a consistently higher peak viral RNA than Omicron BA.1 infections.
evidence: This is a finding from the viral kinetic model stratified by antibody titer.

claim: Among Omicron BA.1 infections, high antibody titers were associated with faster viral clearance times and lower peak viral RNA.
source: Among Omicron BA.1 infections, high antibody titers were associated with faster viral clearance times and lower peak viral RNA.
evidence: This is a finding from the viral kinetic model stratified by antibody titer.

claim: Proliferation times were similar across variants and titers.
source: Proliferation times were similar across variants and titers (Appendix 1—table 6).
evidence: This is a finding from the viral kinetic model.

claim: Symptomatic boosted individuals demonstrated longer clearance times than asymptomatic boosted individuals.
source: We found the same pattern of longer clearance times for boosted individuals relative to fully vaccinated individuals, with symptomatic boosted individuals demonstrating longer clearance times than asymptomatic boosted individuals (Appendix 1—table 7).
evidence: This is a finding from the viral kinetic model stratified by symptom status.

claim: Among those with low antibody titer, presence of symptoms was associated with higher peak viral RNA and longer clearance times.
source: Among those with low antibody titer, presence of symptoms was associated with higher peak viral RNA and longer clearance times, while for those with high antibody titer, peak viral RNA and clearance times were similar between symptom statuses (Appendix 1—table 8).
evidence: This is a finding from the viral kinetic model stratified by antibody titer and symptom status.

claim: For those with high antibody titer, peak viral RNA and clearance times were similar between symptom statuses.
source: Among those with low antibody titer, presence of symptoms was associated with higher peak viral RNA and longer clearance times, while for those with high antibody titer, peak viral RNA and clearance times were similar between symptom statuses (Appendix 1—table 8).
evidence: This is a finding from the viral kinetic model stratified by antibody titer and symptom status.

claim: Older individuals demonstrated longer average clearance times than younger individuals across vaccination and antibody titer groups.
source: Consistent with the logistic regression results, older individuals demonstrated longer average clearance times than younger individuals across vaccination and antibody titer groups.
evidence: This is a finding from the viral kinetic model stratified by age.

claim: Individuals aged 50+years took between roughly 1–2 days longer to clear than individuals aged 30–50, and 2–3 days longer to clear than individuals under 30.
source: When stratifying by immune status, individuals aged 50+years took between roughly 1–2 days longer to clear than individuals aged 30–50, and 2–3 days longer to clear than individuals under 30 (Appendix 1—table 9 and Appendix 1—table 10).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the viral kinetic model stratified by age.

claim: Individuals with low antibody titer and boosted individuals took 1–2 days longer to clear than individuals with high antibody titer and non-boosted individuals in both the <30 and 30–50 year age groups.
source: However, we still found a consistent effect of antibody titer and booster status on clearance time despite this additional age effect. Individuals with low antibody titer and boosted individuals took 1–2 days longer to clear than individuals with high antibody titer and non-boosted individuals in both the <30 and 30–50 year age groups (Appendix 1—table 9 and Appendix 1—table 10).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the viral kinetic model stratified by age and immune status.

claim: Individuals infected with SARS-CoV-2 often had Ct values <30 beyond the five-day isolation period following SARS-CoV-2 infection currently recommended by the CDC.
source: We found that individuals infected with SARS-CoV-2 often had Ct values <30 beyond the five-day isolation period following SARS-CoV-2 infection currently recommended by the CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2022).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis, with reference to CDC guidelines.

claim: This finding is in line with other studies measuring Ct values from upper respiratory tract samples, the duration of antigen test positivity, and the duration of infectious viral load or culturable virus.
source: This finding is in line with other studies measuring Ct values from upper respiratory tract samples, the duration of antigen test positivity, and the duration of infectious viral load or culturable virus (Boucau et al., 2022a; Earnest et al., 2022; Ke et al., 2022; Landon et al., 2022; Lefferts et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Nearly half of the individuals in this cohort had potentially infectious viral loads (Ct <30) five days after their initial detection, even in those detected later in their infection course.
source: While we do not have data on infectiousness by day to clarify the exact link between Ct and infectiousness, nearly half of the individuals in this cohort had potentially infectious viral loads (Ct <30) five days after their initial detection, even in those detected later in their infection course (Singanayagam et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis, with a citation for the Ct-infectiousness relationship.

claim: Low Ct values consistent with potential infectiousness were sometimes maintained for up to two weeks.
source: The duration of positivity was highly variable across individuals, and low Ct values consistent with potential infectiousness were sometimes maintained for up to two weeks.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis of viral trajectories.

claim: These observations suggest the use of test-based, rather than time-based, protocols for defining the duration of isolation to limit the spread of SARS-CoV-2.
source: These observations suggest the use of test-based, rather than time-based, protocols for defining the duration of isolation to limit the spread of SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study's findings.

claim: Rebounds with recurrence of symptoms and positive rapid antigen tests after a period of negative test results have been increasingly reported in individuals treated with SARS-CoV-2 antiviral drugs.
source: Rebounds with recurrence of symptoms and positive rapid antigen tests after a period of negative test results have been increasingly reported in individuals treated with SARS-CoV-2 antiviral drugs (Boucau et al., 2022b; Charness et al., 2022), but estimates for the frequency of viral rebounds in the absence of antiviral treatment have been lacking.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on rebounds after antiviral treatment.

claim: Estimates for the frequency of viral rebounds in the absence of antiviral treatment have been lacking.
source: Rebounds with recurrence of symptoms and positive rapid antigen tests after a period of negative test results have been increasingly reported in individuals treated with SARS-CoV-2 antiviral drugs (Boucau et al., 2022b; Charness et al., 2022), but estimates for the frequency of viral rebounds in the absence of antiviral treatment have been lacking.
evidence: This describes a gap in the literature that the study addresses.

claim: More rebounds were detected when using less stringent Ct value-based definitions.
source: However, more rebounds were detected when using less stringent Ct value-based definitions and were more frequent in Omicron BA.1-infected or boosted individuals, occurring in ~6% of infections in contrast to ~1% of infections in the pre-booster pre-Omicron phase of the pandemic.
evidence: This is a finding from the rebound analysis using different definitions.

claim: Rebounds were more frequent in Omicron BA.1-infected or boosted individuals, occurring in ~6% of infections in contrast to ~1% of infections in the pre-booster pre-Omicron phase of the pandemic.
source: However, more rebounds were detected when using less stringent Ct value-based definitions and were more frequent in Omicron BA.1-infected or boosted individuals, occurring in ~6% of infections in contrast to ~1% of infections in the pre-booster pre-Omicron phase of the pandemic.
evidence: This is a finding from the rebound analysis comparing different phases of the pandemic.

claim: It was not routine for testing to continue following suspected clearance in this cohort, and thus these results may represent a lower bound on the incidence of rebound infections.
source: It was not routine for testing to continue following suspected clearance in this cohort, and thus these results may represent a lower bound on the incidence of rebound infections.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: The frequency of viral trajectory rebounds depends on the definition of 'rebound', highlighting the need for standardized definitions to enable comparisons across studies.
source: The frequency of viral trajectory rebounds depends on the definition of 'rebound', highlighting the need for standardized definitions to enable comparisons across studies.
evidence: This is an interpretation and recommendation based on the study's findings.
